content:
On accuracy, the evidence is mixed. Bonilla López et al. (2018) found that metalinguistic codes were effective for enhancing learners' immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy during text revision. Liu and Wu (2019) found that students favoured direct correction in conjunction with metalinguistic explanations (215/447, 48.10%), followed by direct correction without metalinguistic explanations (111/447, 24.83%). Razmi and Ghane (2024) reported that direct unfocused WCF improved writing performance (d = 1.32), but their design did not provide revision opportunities, and the authors speculated that engaging learners in revision can boost the effect of direct WCF.

On engagement, Bonilla López et al. (2018) found that a mental-effort measure of cognitive load was significantly lower when learners processed direct corrections targeting grammatical issues, implying that metalinguistic codes impose greater processing demands. Koltovskaia (2022) observed that teachers provided feedback on both higher-order and lower-order concerns despite using Grammarly as a complement, with no division of labour.

Mao et al. (2024) reported that low-proficiency learners preferred explicit direct correction while high-proficiency learners regarded less explicit WCF, such as underlining and error codes, as helpful.

quotes: Main results from mixed-effect linear models showed that although direct corrections and codes were effective to enhance learners’ immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy (i.e., during text revision), a long-term advantage (i.e., four weeks after feedback provision) was only evident for direct corrections.

During text revision, experimental groups DCF+G (p < 0.001, SE = 0.069), ME+G (p = 0.009, SE = 0.070), DCF+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.070), and ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.070) significantly outperformed the control group.
The same was true for ME+GN, which significantly outperformed the SC (p < 0.001, SE = 0.060), DCF+G (p < 0.001, SE = 0.059), and ME+G groups (p < 0.001, SE = 0.059).

Low intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) were randomly assigned to four experimental conditions (direct corrections on grammatical errors, metalinguistic codes on grammatical errors, direct corrections on grammatical and non-grammatical errors, or metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors) and a control group (self-correction).

verifications.claim_text: metalinguistic codes were effective for enhancing learners' immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy during text revision
verifications.explanation: The claim's central assertion — that metalinguistic codes enhanced learners' immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy during text revision — is supported by the abstract's statement that "direct corrections and codes were effective to enhance learners’ immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy (i.e., during text revision)". The results section confirms this for both code conditions: ME+G significantly outperformed the control group on grammatical errors successfully corrected (p = 0.009), and ME+GN significantly outperformed the control group on both grammatical (p < 0.001) and non-grammatical (p < 0.001) errors successfully corrected. The peripheral assertions (entity: low-intermediate EFL writers; measure: errors successfully corrected during revision; direction: effective/enhanced) are all supported, and no assertion is contradicted. The claim's plural "codes" is licensed by the source's own plural usage ("codes were effective"), and the source's hedge-free phrasing matches the claim's force.

verifications.explanation: The central assertion is stated almost verbatim in the abstract: "A mental-effort based measure of cognitive load revealed that learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues." The results section confirms this with the post-hoc comparison "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)" and Table 3 ("***ME+GN > DCF+G 1.91 [0.95, 2.88]"). The claim's interpretive gloss that metalinguistic codes impose greater processing demands is also present in the discussion, which attributes the higher load of metalinguistic CF to its problem-solving nature and lower degree of explicitness. No assertion is contradicted and no peripheral assertion is absent, so the claim is verified.

uncited_sentences.sentence: Metalinguistic coded feedback—error codes or brief explanatory labels supplied without the correct form—occupies a distinctive position among written corrective feedback (WCF) types because it demands that learners infer the target form rather than copy it.
The studies reviewed here address its accuracy effects, its processing costs, and learner preferences for it relative to direct correction, automated feedback, and peer feedback.
On accuracy, the evidence is mixed.

Across these studies, metalinguistic coded feedback appears to support revision and to suit more proficient learners, yet its accuracy advantage over direct correction remains unclear, and its processing costs are inferred from a single cognitive-load measure.

The same review noted that most naturalistic WCF studies were qualitative (66.0%) and that only 11 of 50 articles (22.0%) made explicit reference to theoretical tenets, and it excluded research on feedback from peers and computational tools.
